prompt: In a `Nested Loop`, which child runs once per row of the other?

choices.text: The first child printed
choices.why: That is the outer side; it runs once.

choices.text: The second child printed, the inner side
choices.why: Right: in customer 4242's join it shows loops=10, one per order.

choices.text: Whichever child has an index
choices.why: Both children can use indexes; the position decides which repeats.

choices.text: Neither: both run once and are compared row by row
choices.why: That describes a merge join.

prompt: The inner index scan shows `rows=2 loops=10` and `Buffers: shared hit=15 read=25`. How many pages did all ten lookups touch together?

choices.text: 400: 40 per loop times 10
choices.why: Buffers are already summed over the loops; only times and rows are per loop.

choices.text: 40 in all, about 4 per lookup
choices.why: Right: unlike rows and times, the buffer counts are totals.

choices.text: 20, one per row returned
choices.why: Each lookup walked index levels too; the count is 40.

choices.text: 25, since the 15 hits were not touched
choices.why: A hit is a page touched in memory; it counts.

prompt: An inner index scan takes about 0.022 ms per loop. Roughly how many milliseconds would 100000 outer rows cost in lookups alone?
A nested loop's outer child shows `rows=12` estimated and `rows=95000` actual, and its inner index scan `loops=95000`. What is the cause to chase first?
hint: Which number was the loop chosen on?

choices.text: The index on the inner side is missing
choices.why: It exists: the inner side is an index scan.

choices.text: The outer estimate, 12 against 95000
choices.why: Right: the join was right for 12 rows; the estimate was wrong.

choices.text: work_mem is too small to hold the loop
choices.why: A nested loop holds no hash table; work_mem does not limit it.

choices.text: Parallel plans were switched off for the session
choices.why: Parallelism would split the work, not change the 95000 lookups.

prompt: Which input of a hash join is read into the hash table?

choices.text: The bigger one, so the probes are fewer
choices.why: The opposite: hashing the bigger side costs more memory and more batches.

choices.text: Always the left table of the SQL
choices.why: The planner picks the side; customers were hashed though written second.

choices.text: The smaller, by the estimate
choices.why: Right: 200000 customers rather than two million orders.

choices.text: Both, into one table
choices.why: One side builds, the other probes.

prompt: A `Hash` node shows `Batches: 2  Memory Usage: 5966kB` and the join `temp read=3262 written=3262`. What does that say?
hint: Memory allowed is work_mem times a multiplier.

choices.text: It did not fit, and part went to disk
choices.why: Right: the hash outgrew its memory, and about 25 MB went to temporary files and back.

choices.text: Two processes built the hash in parallel
choices.why: Batches are parts of one hash, not workers; parallel plans were off.

choices.text: The join ran twice over the same input
choices.why: loops=1; the batches are passes over split data.

choices.text: Shared buffers were full at the time
choices.why: Temp files belong to work_mem, not to shared buffers.

prompt: With `work_mem` at 32 MB the customers' hash fitted in one batch and the query took 1401 ms; at 1 MB it took 8 batches and 943 ms. What should you conclude before raising `work_mem` on the server?
hint: Did the spill cost what the planner thought?

choices.text: More memory makes hash joins slower, so lower it on the server
choices.why: One query on one warm machine does not show a rule in either direction.

choices.text: The timings are wrong because ANALYZE adds overhead
choices.why: All three paid the same overhead.

choices.text: Batches above 1 must be removed whatever they cost
choices.why: Here removing them bought nothing; they are a cost to measure, not a verdict.

choices.text: Batches are a cost to measure, and here the spill was cheap
choices.why: Right: the temp files stayed in the OS cache; measure, and weigh every connection's share.

prompt: A hash may use `work_mem` times `hash_mem_multiplier`, which is ___ by default.
What does a merge join need from its two inputs?

choices.text: Sorted on the join key
choices.why: Right: then each is walked once, together.

choices.text: An index on each table's primary key, whatever the join
choices.why: Order is what it needs; an index is only one way to get it.

choices.text: Small enough for work_mem
choices.why: That is the hash join's need.

choices.text: The same number of rows on each side
choices.why: 200000 orders met 500001 lines.

prompt: The merge join's index scan of `order_lines` shows `rows=500001` although the table has five million. Why?

choices.text: The statistics were stale
choices.why: Estimates were close; rows= here is what was read.

choices.text: It stopped past order 200000
choices.why: Right: one row past the last match ended the join.

choices.text: Only half a million lines have an order
choices.why: Every line has an order; the other lines belong to later orders.

choices.text: An index-only scan returns one row per page
choices.why: It returns every matching entry.

prompt: The planner chose a hash join (1392 ms) over a merge join (171 ms), with estimates within 1% of the truth. Setting `random_page_cost = 1.1` made it pick the merge. What do you take from that?
hint: Rows were right; something else was priced wrong.

choices.text: Put enable_hashjoin = off in the configuration
choices.why: That forces every join and leaves the wrong price in place.

choices.text: Run ANALYZE so the estimates improve
choices.why: The estimates were already right: 504377 against 500000.

choices.text: A price was wrong, not a row count
choices.why: Right: random_page_cost overcharges index reads on this cached machine; measure it and set it once in the configuration.

choices.text: Merge joins are always faster than hash joins
choices.why: Only when the inputs are already in order; here they were.

prompt: Joining customers to their orders, the planner used a nested loop for 10 and 1000 customers and a hash join for 20000. What changed between them?

choices.text: The indexes available
choices.why: The same indexes existed for all three.

choices.text: The expected number of outer rows
choices.why: Right: the loop's cost grows with them and the hash join's barely does.

choices.text: The work_mem setting
choices.why: It was the default in all three.

choices.text: The order of the tables in the SQL
choices.why: The SQL was the same apart from the number.

prompt: At 1000 customers the planner expected 1027 outer rows and priced one inner lookup at 36.75. Roughly what is the nested loop's cost, before the small extras?
In the hash join for 20000 customers, why are the customers the hashed side?

choices.text: 20000 rows make a smaller table than two million
choices.why: Right: the planner hashes the side it expects to be smaller.

choices.text: customers is written first in the query
choices.why: Written order does not decide; estimates do.

choices.text: orders has no index the hash can use
choices.why: A hash join uses no index on either side.

choices.text: A hash join may only hash a table with a primary key
choices.why: Any input can be hashed; keys play no part.

prompt: Match each warning sign to the join it belongs to.
hint: The last table of the lesson.

pairs.left: `loops` in the thousands where few were expected
a `Sort` in front of each input

prompt: A join is slow. Put these steps in the order the lesson teaches you to take them.
items: Compare estimated and actual rows on the join's children, from the bottom
If the estimates hold, force the rejected method to compare
Question the price list or the indexes, not the join
trap: Forcing a method first skips the question of whether the estimate was the cause.

prompt: Which of these are true of the three join methods? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A nested loop's cost grows with the outer rows
choices.why: Right: rows times one lookup.

choices.text: A hash join reads each side once
choices.why: Right: build once, probe once.

choices.text: A merge join's output comes out sorted on the key
choices.why: Right: an ORDER BY on it costs nothing extra.

choices.text: A hash join needs an index on the join column
choices.why: It uses no index.

choices.text: A merge join cannot stop before the end of either input
choices.why: It stopped at order 200000 in the lesson.

prompt: A report joins a 300-row `regions` table to a 40-million-row `sales` table on `region_id`, with no filter, and `sales` has an index on `region_id`. Which method do you expect, and why?

choices.text: A nested loop over the regions, using the index on sales
choices.why: 300 lookups would together fetch all 40 million rows in index order, the slow way.

choices.text: A merge join, because region_id is indexed
choices.why: Only one side is in order, and the 40 million would have to be walked through the index.

choices.text: A hash join on the 300 regions
choices.why: Right: the 300 regions are hashed in memory and sales is read once, in order.

choices.text: No join: the planner reads both and filters
choices.why: A join needs one of the three methods.
